newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton seen mixed in Pakistan and India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton seen mixed in Pakistan and India.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to remain depressed in Pakistan and mixed in neighbouring India in the current week, dealers said Friday.

In Pakistan, the prices are likely to remain depressed as the government has not withdrawn 10 percent sales tax that will not encourage exporters to buy cotton, broker Nasim Usman at the private Karachi Cotton Association said.
He said exporters were expecting withdrawal of the tax from cotton in an economic reforms package announced by Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz on Friday.
Pakistan's cotton export fell to 31,647 bales (375 lbs each) between September 1, 1996 and March 24 from 1.594 million in the year-ago period.
The tax had increased domestic rates that are incompetitive abroad, Usman said

"There should be no sales tax on the export of cotton," KCA chairman Nadershaw D. Kabraji said after the announcement of the package, which reduced sales tax on several items and income and corporate taxes.
"As a policy matter the KCA demands that there should not be any sales tax on primary agricultural commodities."
Cotton rates in Pakistan closed steady on Friday owing to low buying by textile mills, dealers said.
The rates fluctuated slightly in the kerb market where mills with ready cash bought at a rate lower than at the KCA, one dealer said.
In the kerb market, the NIAB-78 variety was quoted 2,100/2,250 rupees per maund (37.32 kg), the K-68 at 2,450/2,475 and the MNH-93 at 2,460/2,485, he said.
The prices are likely to fall in the next few days as ginners, who were holding 1.446 million bales of unsold stocks until Thursday, plan to sell, the dealer said.

In India, the prices are expected to rule mixed in the current week in subdued trade, dealers there said.
They said prices of cotton varieties from India's western state of Gujarat firmed on buying by authorities to appease farmers before a local election there.

In the week to Thursday, the Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) rose 400/500 rupees to 13,000/13,500 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and the Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) gained 500/1,000 rupees to 19,000/20,000 rupees per candy.
The Punjab saw-ginned fell 60 rupees to 1,500/1,650 rupees per maund (37.32 kg), the Bengal-deshi 10 rupees to 870/920, and the F-414 variety 40 rupees to 1,880/1,900 rupees.

Manubhai Amarsey, a leading cotton trader, said supplies from Gujarat and northern India were low and trading volumes small during the week as most players kept to the sidelines amid hectic closing of year-end accounts.
The fiscal 1996/97 ends on March 31.
"Market sentiment is also dull on reports that the Indian government is considering to allow more export of value-added items such as cotton yarn instead of raw cotton," Amarsey said.
($1 = 40.22 Pakistani rupees)
